status: Research-led design proposal only; no focus, event, spirit, modifier, or loaded-game edits
title: France 1970: differentiated right-centre foreign and military programmes
period: 1970-1990, with named post-1970 developments available only from their historical dates

design_rules.factuality: Historical facts are cited in source notes; any new policy, offer, or spirit is identified as a plausible alternate-history proposal.
design_rules.offers: Each named partner proposal is unlocked by a French focus and sent to that country. The recipient gets explicit Accept and Decline decisions. Acceptance applies both national spirits together; refusal applies neither. These are bilateral proposals, not historical claims that the agreement existed.
design_rules.spirit_lifecycle: Accepted spirits are continuing rather than fixed-term. Keep both active only while neither signatory is at war with the other and neither has an active bilateral sanction against the other. War, a sanction in either direction, withdrawal, or signatory removal ends both spirits together. No automatic acceptance, forced alliance, or nuclear sharing.
design_rules.mechanics: Describe effects as policy outcomes and opportunity costs. Do not invent executable MD modifier keys or promise numerical values. Calibrate any later game effects against installed MD providers and readers.
design_rules.research: Use narrow extensions of the current France 1970 research lanes, with exact reachable technology IDs and actual DLC/project requirements verified before implementation. A design programme must not complete a special project or grant a broad category bonus by implication.
design_rules.party_identity: Keep each path attached to its existing exact France subparty and date/identity guards. Do not introduce party slots or conflate 1970 Radical currents across the 1972-73 split.

party_paths.period_identity: UDR under Pompidou at the January 1970 start; RPR only after its 1976 formation under Chirac.

strategic_fork.question: Should Gaullist modernization buy European scale through industrial workshare, or preserve a more nationally controlled procurement and readiness base?

options.name: Continental Modernisation
options.historical_fact: French-West German Airbus Industrie was established in 1970; British Aerospace joined the consortium in 1979. France and the FRG later expanded military consultation and exercises.
options.plausible_choice: Extend civil-industrial workshare into selected conventional interoperability and joint officer preparation.
options.benefit: Larger production and export markets, broader technical inputs, and more interoperable conventional forces.
options.cost: Workshare constraints, dependence on partner production schedules, and recurring coordination costs; no partner gains a say over French nuclear release.

options.name: National Direction
options.historical_fact: UDR speakers defended the national deterrent, territorial defense, and military modernization in parliamentary debates.
options.plausible_choice: Keep procurement choices and force planning under stronger national direction, accepting higher public capital commitments and fewer shared production economies.
options.benefit: Greater control over force design and supply priorities.
options.cost: Higher fiscal exposure and weaker access to partner workshare and export networks.

strategic_fork.military_path: Deepen mechanized readiness and tactical-aircraft integration around the existing AMX-30 and fighter programmes; add mobilization, maintenance, and procurement oversight as real alternatives to simply increasing factory output.
narrow_research_lanes: Main Battle Tank Development: the existing 1975 tank/chassis target
Air-Superiority Fighter Development: the existing 1980 light-airframe or 1985 fallback target
Aerospace workshare and maintenance doctrine; do not add an unverified tech ID

offers.name: Continental Air and Land Workshare
offers.historical_anchor: Airbus Industrie was created in 1970 with French and West German partners; joint French-German military exercises and staff cooperation are documented by 1987.
offers.proposal_status: Alternate-history extension from civil-industrial cooperation to selected conventional maintenance, logistics, and staff standards.

france_spirit.benefit: Improved access to continental production, supplier capacity, and conventional interoperability.
france_spirit.cost: Shared workshare reduces freedom to redirect production unilaterally and deepens reliance on partner schedules.

partner_spirit.benefit: Access to French aerospace and land-systems expertise and a standing consultation channel.
partner_spirit.cost: Accepts France's autonomous command and receives no nuclear co-decision.

offers.name: Anglo-French Aerospace and Maritime Standards
offers.historical_anchor: The United Kingdom participated in Concorde and British industry supplied Airbus wings from the programme's early years; British Aerospace joined the Airbus consortium in 1979.
offers.proposal_status: Alternate-history expansion of actual aerospace collaboration into reciprocal training and maritime-rescue procedures; not a joint combat-aircraft procurement claim.

france_spirit.benefit: Civil-aerospace exports, shared engineering knowledge, and more compatible maritime rescue practice.
france_spirit.cost: Workshare and export priorities can compete with French-led programmes and consume public development funds.

partner_spirit.benefit: Continued access to French airframe and systems expertise and shared aerospace markets.
partner_spirit.cost: Industrial commitments expose both sides to export-cycle and programme-delay risk.

offers.name: Sovereign Détente Consultations
offers.historical_anchor: France and the USSR signed a political-consultation protocol in October 1970; French-Soviet exchanges continued in science, technology, culture, and trade.
offers.proposal_status: Plausible expansion of consultation and civilian scientific exchange; excludes weapons design, intelligence sharing, and alliance commitments.

france_spirit.benefit: Additional diplomatic leverage and civilian scientific or industrial contacts.
france_spirit.cost: Alliance friction and greater exposure to technology-security disputes.

partner_spirit.benefit: A durable Western European consultation channel and selected civilian exchanges.
partner_spirit.cost: The channel recognizes France's independent course and does not weaken French ties with Western allies.

party_paths.period_identity: Michel Debré and sovereignty-first Gaullist networks; retain the distinction from the governing UDR's more technocratic modernization line.

strategic_fork.question: Should scarce resources protect the independent deterrent and national command first, or build a larger conventional intervention capacity while retaining that deterrent?

options.name: Independent Deterrence First
options.historical_fact: Debré argued in 1970 for deterrence as the core of defense, with independent national decision-making.
options.plausible_choice: Prioritize strategic-submarine continuity, command resilience, and domestic control of sensitive systems.
options.benefit: Credible sovereign decision-making and protected strategic-industrial expertise.
options.cost: Capital-intensive undersea programmes constrain conventional readiness and social or civil spending.

options.name: Intervention as the Deterrent's Shield
options.historical_fact: Debré also argued that France needed forces capable of limited intervention and could not be neutral about European or Mediterranean security.
options.plausible_choice: Maintain the independent deterrent while directing more resources to conventional mobility, reserves, and overseas logistics.
options.benefit: A credible response below the nuclear threshold and greater freedom to act with or without partners.
options.cost: Higher personnel, lift, and sustainment burdens; conventional expansion competes with the strategic force.

strategic_fork.military_path: A sovereignty-first undersea and command path versus a costly conventional mobility/intervention complement. Foreign agreements may consult and train but never transfer French nuclear authority.
narrow_research_lanes: Submarine Engineering: existing 1980 Attack Submarine Hull II target
Main Battle Tank Development: existing 1975 tank/chassis target
Command resilience, secure communications, and force mobility as design themes; require exact local technology validation

offers.name: Rhineland Crisis Consultation
offers.historical_anchor: Franco-German defense clauses were reactivated through ministerial meetings and a security commission from 1982; large-scale exercises and officer training followed in 1987.
offers.proposal_status: A plausible sovereignty-first compact: joint threat assessment and conventional exercises, with an explicit no-nuclear-delegation rule.

france_spirit.benefit: Better warning, conventional coordination, and direct influence over European security debate.
france_spirit.cost: More disclosure of French conventional posture and recurring staff commitments.

partner_spirit.benefit: Improved consultation with a nearby nuclear ally and more compatible conventional planning.
partner_spirit.cost: Accepts that French forces remain outside NATO's integrated command and French nuclear decisions remain national.

offers.name: Political Détente and Civil Science Protocol
offers.historical_anchor: A French-Soviet consultation protocol dates to October 1970; archives describe civilian medical, nuclear-energy, and space-science cooperation during détente.
offers.proposal_status: Keep it civilian and reversible; no weapons research, shared intelligence, or military technology transfers.

france_spirit.benefit: Additional diplomatic access and selected civilian research opportunities.
france_spirit.cost: Political and technology-security risk, with possible alliance mistrust.

partner_spirit.benefit: Regular high-level consultation and civilian technical exchange with an independent Western power.
partner_spirit.cost: No strategic alignment or control over France's independent deterrent.

offers.name: Alliance Deconfliction Without Integration
offers.historical_anchor: Mitterrand stated in 1987 that France belonged to the Atlantic Alliance but not its integrated command and retained autonomous deterrence while meeting alliance obligations.
offers.proposal_status: Explicit counterfactual crisis-communications compact that tests whether an orthodox government can reduce miscalculation without returning to integrated command.

france_spirit.benefit: Lower risk of allied misreading during a European crisis and stronger conventional coordination.
france_spirit.cost: Greater transparency and domestic criticism that autonomy is being diluted.

partner_spirit.benefit: Clearer crisis signals from France and better consultation with a major European ally.
partner_spirit.cost: Washington accepts no command authority over French forces and no nuclear-sharing arrangement.

party_paths.period_identity: Independent Republicans in the 1970s; UDF is a 1978 coalition, not a January 1970 party label.

strategic_fork.question: Should liberal modernization favor competitive procurement and export partnerships, or use fiscal stabilization to constrain defense commitments and protect macroeconomic room?

options.name: Competitive European Procurement
options.historical_fact: Giscard's government helped launch the European Monetary System in 1979 and promoted international economic coordination; Airbus expanded British participation in 1979.
options.plausible_choice: Compete through avionics, aircraft integration, and export-oriented joint programmes rather than duplicating every platform nationally.
options.benefit: Technology access, export scale, and stronger supplier productivity.
options.cost: External workshare, import dependence, and volatile export demand.

options.name: Stabilise Before Expanding
options.historical_fact: Giscard-era diplomacy emphasized monetary stability and coordination after the oil shock.
options.plausible_choice: Set a hard fiscal envelope, preserve specialist cadres and maintenance, and defer prestige procurement when it crowds out balance-of-payments or social priorities.
options.benefit: Greater budget credibility and less risk of unfunded procurement commitments.
options.cost: Slower force renewal, readiness gaps, and domestic industry pressure.

strategic_fork.military_path: Competitive multirole aircraft and microelectronics with professional technical cadres; contrast open supplier competition with an explicit readiness-and-maintenance budget ceiling.
narrow_research_lanes: Multirole Aircraft Development: existing 1980 medium-airframe or 1985 fallback target
Aircraft design project remains required where the active native branch requires it

offers.name: Monetary and Civil-Technology Consultation
offers.historical_anchor: Giscard convened the 1975 Rambouillet G6; the leaders discussed common economic problems and France and the United States reached agreement on international monetary reform.
offers.proposal_status: Counterfactual continuing bilateral channel extending the summit precedent into civilian computing, energy, and crisis consultation.

france_spirit.benefit: More predictable economic consultation and access to civilian research contacts.
france_spirit.cost: Exposure to US market and technology dependence and pressure to align policy.

partner_spirit.benefit: Earlier coordination with France on trade, currency, and civilian technical standards.
partner_spirit.cost: France retains freedom to dissent and does not promise military alignment.

offers.name: European Monetary and Supplier Standards Compact
offers.historical_anchor: The EMS entered into force in March 1979 with French-German leadership; French and West German companies were the initial Airbus Industrie partners.
offers.proposal_status: Counterfactual extension from monetary coordination to shared supplier qualification and aircraft-electronics research.

france_spirit.benefit: More stable investment planning and access to a large industrial supplier base.
france_spirit.cost: Less freedom to use procurement as a protected national market and tighter exposure to German economic priorities.

partner_spirit.benefit: More predictable French procurement and access to French aerospace integration.
partner_spirit.cost: Shared standards and funding commitments limit unilateral programme changes.

offers.name: British Civil-Aerospace Market Accord
offers.historical_anchor: British Aerospace acquired a 20 percent Airbus stake in January 1979 after British industrial participation in Airbus wing production.
offers.proposal_status: Alternate-history extension to training, export certification, and selected non-sensitive avionics research.

france_spirit.benefit: Broader export access and private-sector engineering competition.
france_spirit.cost: Public programmes become more exposed to partner commercial priorities and procurement rivalry.

partner_spirit.benefit: Stable French market access and common export-campaign procedures.
partner_spirit.cost: Acceptance ties UK industry to a shared workshare and development schedule.

party_paths.period_identity: Jean Lecanuet's Centre démocrate becomes the CDS in 1976; the UDF brings the centre family together in 1978.

strategic_fork.question: Should France move toward collective European conventional planning and a reformed Atlantic alliance, or preserve a primarily national command structure with only selective coordination?

options.name: European Security With Parliamentary Oversight
options.historical_fact: Lecanuet argued in 1970 for collective European defense and, in 1973, criticized the slow advance of European unity and sought renewed security cooperation.
options.plausible_choice: Prioritize joint officer education, conventional interoperability, maritime escort, and parliamentary review of commitments.
options.benefit: Partner confidence and greater conventional coordination.
options.cost: Negotiation delays and less freedom to act without consultation.

options.name: National Command, Selective Solidarity
options.historical_fact: France's strategic doctrine remained nationally controlled even as later governments expanded European cooperation.
options.plausible_choice: Retain national command and deterrence while limiting joint commitments to practical missions and civil protection.
options.benefit: Preserves national decision time while keeping functional ties.
options.cost: Less influence over collective planning and fewer pooled capabilities.

strategic_fork.military_path: Joint-service readiness, frigate escort and territorial civil-defense/reserve service; choose broad European consultation or nationally bounded participation, rather than a generic combat bonus.
narrow_research_lanes: Infantry Support Weapons: existing 1970/1978 support targets
Joint-service communications, naval escort doctrine, and civil-defense engineering

offers.name: Franco-German Officer and Crisis-Consultation Protocol
offers.historical_anchor: The military provisions of the Élysée Treaty were activated from 1982; by 1987 France and the FRG held major exercises and developed common officer training.
offers.proposal_status: A plausible CDS-led early or deeper extension with reciprocal recipient consent; do not call it a joint nuclear force.

france_spirit.benefit: More compatible staff procedures and influence over European crisis consultation.
france_spirit.cost: Joint planning consumes officer time and can constrain unilateral movement.

partner_spirit.benefit: French participation in practical conventional defense and an enduring political channel.
partner_spirit.cost: Germany accepts French nuclear autonomy and distinct command arrangements.

offers.name: Benelux Civil Protection and Border-Service Compact
offers.historical_anchor: France and Belgium were founding EEC members; the 1985 Schengen Agreement among Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands later established a border-cooperation precedent.
offers.proposal_status: Plausible bilateral extension for emergency communications, engineering support, and port/rail contingency planning; not a claim of an existing French-Belgian military pact.

france_spirit.benefit: Faster civil-defense coordination and better access to neighboring transport routes.
france_spirit.cost: Shared procedures and cross-border readiness obligations require sustained local investment.

partner_spirit.benefit: French engineering and emergency capacity for cross-border incidents.
partner_spirit.cost: Requires compatible procedures and reciprocal access, with no guarantee of French intervention in a war.

offers.name: Mediterranean Escort and Rescue Understanding
offers.historical_anchor: France and Italy both participated in the 1975 Rambouillet economic summit; broader European consultation grew during the period.
offers.proposal_status: Counterfactual practical agreement for maritime rescue, convoy coordination in peacetime, and naval medical evacuation; no automatic defense guarantee.

france_spirit.benefit: More reliable Mediterranean rescue and escort cooperation.
france_spirit.cost: Naval readiness and exercises compete with Atlantic and overseas commitments.

partner_spirit.benefit: French coordination and improved maritime emergency capacity.
partner_spirit.cost: Must accept that mission participation remains nationally approved and limited to the agreed scope.

party_paths.period_identity: Treat the 1972-73 rupture as a real fork: Servan-Schreiber's reformist/current-centrist path differs from Fabre and Faure's left-radical MRG path. The current single party slot cannot be assumed to represent both after the split without checking its dated identity.

strategic_fork.question: Should a radical government cut prestige and subsidy-heavy defense commitments to fund regional public services, or preserve a smaller but credible territorial and technical force while pursuing civilian reform more gradually?

options.name: Reinvest in Regions and Civilian Engineering
options.historical_fact: In 1975 Servan-Schreiber argued for reducing unproductive subsidies and military expenditure while increasing collective services and local-government investment.
options.plausible_choice: Convert selected industrial and engineering capacity toward transport, civil protection, environmental monitoring, and regional infrastructure.
options.benefit: Visible civilian capacity and regional development.
options.cost: Readiness, procurement continuity, and defense-industry employment become harder to sustain.

options.name: A Lean Territorial Guarantee
options.historical_fact: Radical leaders contested defense doctrine; the historical record does not support a single unified radical military platform through the party split.
options.plausible_choice: Keep a limited engineering, reserve, and civil-defense structure while negotiating European and municipal partnerships.
options.benefit: Preserves a practical response capacity and offers a compromise to allies and defense workers.
options.cost: Reduces the fiscal room for rapid regional-service expansion; neither the deterrent nor overseas forces receive automatic upgrades.

strategic_fork.military_path: Engineer mobility, communications and instrumentation, territorial reserve training, and civil-defense service. Treat nuclear-policy change as a separate contested political decision; do not infer automatic disarmament.
narrow_research_lanes: Combat Engineer Equipment: existing 1968 engineer-vehicle target
Civil-protection, environmental instrumentation, and dual-use transport research

offers.name: Franco-Belgian Municipal Resilience Exchange
offers.historical_anchor: France and Belgium were EEC founding members; subsequent European cross-border agreements provide an institutional precedent, while no specific 1970s radical-led resilience compact is documented.
offers.proposal_status: Explicitly counterfactual exchange between municipalities on flood response, public transit, and civil-engineering standards.

france_spirit.benefit: Regional engineering knowledge and stronger municipal emergency planning.
france_spirit.cost: Local authorities must fund shared standards and reserve capacity.

partner_spirit.benefit: Access to French civil-engineering expertise and reciprocal municipal practice.
partner_spirit.cost: Requires matching local investment and continuing cross-border coordination.

offers.name: French-Italian Urban Mobility and Civil-Protection Accord
offers.historical_anchor: France and Italy shared EEC institutions and the 1975 Rambouillet economic dialogue; the environmental and urban-policy exchange is an alternate-history proposal, not a documented state agreement.
offers.proposal_status: Peacetime knowledge-sharing on public transport, coastal emergency response, and municipal engineering; no defense guarantee.

france_spirit.benefit: Urban and coastal resilience expertise with a Mediterranean partner.
france_spirit.cost: Engineering resources are diverted from military construction and central procurement priorities.

partner_spirit.benefit: Access to French planning and civil-protection experience.
partner_spirit.cost: Reciprocity requires French access to partner practices and sustained public funding.

offers.name: Iberian Regional Democracy and Engineering Partnership
offers.historical_anchor: Spain joined the European Communities on 1 January 1986 after its democratic transition; the proposed regional-democracy and civil-engineering accord is a plausible extension, not a historical treaty.
offers.proposal_status: Date-gated exchange on decentralized services, transport engineering, and civil protection, open only after Spain's accession date in this scenario.

france_spirit.benefit: Stronger southwestern links and practical regional-governance cooperation.
france_spirit.cost: Requires cross-border investment and may divert resources from centralized defense procurement.

partner_spirit.benefit: French technical support and stronger institutional access to a neighboring Community member.
partner_spirit.cost: Accepts reciprocal review and shared standards rather than unilateral project control.

implementation_gate: Design review only.
